cards.question: What is a path, like ../data/teddy.obj?
answers: The address of a file through its folders
A route that starts where you are: one folder up, into data, the file teddy.obj
The contents of the file teddy.obj
A web address that only works online
cards.explanation: A path names the folders to walk through. One that starts from where you are, with .. for one folder up, is a relative path and keeps working if the whole course folder moves.

cards.question: What is the working directory?
answers: The folder you are in right now
The folder from which relative paths start
Always the top folder /
The folder where Python is installed
cards.explanation: pwd prints it, cd changes it. In a notebook it is the folder of the notebook, which is why mkdir -p my_files in the terminal needed a cd first.

cards.question: Which of these is true of a text file?
answers: It holds only characters, line after line
A number read from it comes back as text until you convert it
It always knows which of its values are numbers
It can only hold words, never 3D models
cards.explanation: '14.5' read from my_room.txt is text; float() makes it a number. The teddy OBJ is a text file too: v lines for points, f lines for triangles.

cards.question: What does the header of a file do?
answers: It says what kind of file this is, in its first line or lines
It lets a reader check it got the right kind of file before reading on
It holds the actual measurements
It is hidden and only programs can see it
cards.explanation: ROOM FILE in the first line tells a person and a program what follows. In a CSV the first line is a header too: the column names.

cards.question: Why does a file carry a format version, like 'version 2'?
answers: So the reader knows which rules the rest of the file follows
So old files can still be read after the format changes
So the file becomes smaller
So nobody can change the format any more
cards.explanation: read_room looks at the version line first, then reads version 1 line by line and version 2 split at commas. An unknown version 3 makes it stop instead of guessing.

cards.question: What is a CSV file?
answers: A table as text: column names in the first line, one row per line
Values separated by commas, which pandas reads with read_csv
A picture of a spreadsheet
A file only Excel can open
cards.explanation: my_flat.csv is plain text you can cat. pandas reads it in one line and turns columns that look like numbers into numbers.

cards.question: In https://tiss.tuwien.ac.at/course/courseDetails.xhtml?courseNr=259021#groups, which statements are right?
answers: tiss.tuwien.ac.at is the host, the name of the machine
courseNr=259021 is a query parameter
#groups is sent to the server with the request
The port is missing, so the request cannot be sent
cards.explanation: Scheme, host, port, path, query, fragment, always in that order. The fragment stays in the browser, and a missing port means the default: 443 for https.

cards.question: What do the IP address and the DNS do?
answers: The IP address is the number by which machines find each other, like 128.130.32.110
The DNS turns a name like tiss.tuwien.ac.at into that number
The DNS stores the web pages themselves
The IP address is the same as the URL
cards.explanation: Names are for people, numbers for machines. Before your phone can ask TISS for anything, it looks up the number in the DNS, the phone book of the internet.

cards.question: What is a port?
answers: The door on a machine that picks the service
443 for https and 80 for http, unless the URL says otherwise
The cable socket of the server
Another word for the IP address
cards.explanation: One machine can offer web pages, ssh and e-mail at once, each behind its own number. You rarely see a port in a URL because the scheme sets the default; Jupyter on a laptop uses :8888.

cards.question: What is the difference between HTTP GET and POST?
answers: GET asks for something named in the URL
POST sends data in the body of the request, for example a form or a sensor reading
GET is encrypted and POST is not
POST is only used for downloading files
cards.explanation: Everything a GET says sits in the URL, which ends up in histories and logs. That is why passwords travel in the body of a POST, and why encryption is a matter of https, not of the verb.

cards.question: Which statements about status codes are right?
answers: 404 means the server did not find what you asked for
A program checks the status code before it touches the content
A 404 answer never has any content
200 means the data is correct
cards.explanation: TISS answered a missing page with 404 and still sent 12 kB of friendly HTML. 200 only says the request worked, not that what came back is right.

cards.question: What does a query parameter like forecast_days=3 do?
answers: It changes the question you ask the same machine
In Python, requests builds it from a dictionary such as {"forecast_days": 3}
It picks a different server
It is ignored by every server
cards.explanation: With forecast_days=7 the weather service sent 168 hourly values instead of 72; with 30 it said 400, bad request. Same host, same path, a different question.

cards.question: Which of these is true of JSON?
answers: It is text that holds objects in curly braces and lists in square brackets
It knows numbers, text, true, false and null
It hands every value over as text, numbers included
It can only be read by JavaScript
cards.explanation: JSON keeps 11.6 a number and true a boolean. Python reads it with json.loads into a dictionary; every browser has a reader built in too.

cards.question: In {"temperature": 11.6, "unit": "°C"}, read into reading, what is right?
answers: temperature and unit are keys, 11.6 and "°C" their values
reading["temperature"] gives 11.6
reading["Temperature"] also gives 11.6
reading[0] gives 11.6
cards.explanation: You pick a value by its key, letter for letter. A capital T gives a KeyError, and a dictionary has no positions to count.

cards.question: data = {"location": {"lat": 48.2}, "last_three": [11.6, 12.0, 12.4]}. Which lines are right?
answers: data["location"]["lat"] gives 48.2
data["last_three"][0] gives 11.6
data["lat"] gives 48.2
data["last_three"][1] gives 11.6
cards.explanation: Go in step by step: first the outer key, then the inner one. Lists count from 0, so [0] is the first entry.

cards.question: What is an API, like the one the Vienna sensors answer through?
answers: A web address that answers programs with data, usually JSON
Something you ask with an HTTP GET and query parameters such as interval
A web page designed for people to read
A file that must be downloaded and installed first
cards.explanation: An API answers a program, not a person. You can still open its URL in a browser and see the raw JSON.

cards.question: What does R30/2025-10-17T00:00/P1D ask for?
answers: 30 values, one per day, starting 17 October 2025 at midnight
The same 30 days as R60/2025-10-17T00:00/PT12H, cut into days instead of half days
One value for the whole of October 2025
30 values, one per hour
cards.explanation: R is repeat, P is period, T says a time follows: P1D is one day, PT12H twelve hours. Sixty half days are the same thirty days.

cards.question: Which of these is true of XML?
answers: Values sit between an opening and a closing tag, like <temperature>11.6</temperature>
Read with xml.etree, 11.6 comes back as the text '11.6'
It is never used any more
It is always shorter than JSON
cards.explanation: XML hands everything over as text and writes most names twice, in the opening and closing tag. It lives on in gbXML, SVG, KML and inside every .docx file.

cards.question: What does a database give you that a pile of text files does not?
answers: Tables in one place that programs can query, change and share
Links between tables, so a name is written only once
Data that can never be wrong
A faster internet connection
cards.explanation: In the shared log of session 4, two rooms had six spellings. In the database each room is one row, and everything else points at its key. The data can still be wrong; the -40 °C reading went in without complaint.

cards.question: In the table rooms (id, name, floor, area_m2), what is a row and what is a column?
answers: A row is one room
A column is one property, with one kind of value, like area_m2
A row is one property of all rooms
A column is one room
cards.explanation: Row 4 is the studio: floor 2, 95 m². The column floor holds a whole number for every room.

cards.question: The sensor table stores room_id instead of the room name. Why?
answers: room_id is a foreign key: it points at the key of a row in rooms
Renaming a room then changes one row, and every sensor follows
Numbers take less space, which is the main reason
SQL cannot store text
cards.explanation: When the library became the Reading room, one UPDATE was enough; the JOIN showed the new name at once. The key also refused a second room 6 and a sensor in room 99.

cards.question: What does  SELECT name FROM rooms WHERE floor = 2  do?
answers: It asks for the names of the rooms on floor 2
WHERE keeps only the rows for which the condition is true
It moves all rooms to floor 2
It deletes the rooms that are not on floor 2
cards.explanation: SELECT only reads. Changing rows is UPDATE, removing them is DELETE, and both need a WHERE too, or they hit the whole table.

cards.question: What does  sensors JOIN rooms ON sensors.room_id = rooms.id  do?
answers: It glues to each sensor the row of its room
It matches where the foreign key equals the key
It copies all rooms into the sensor table for good
It adds the two tables up
cards.explanation: The JOIN puts back together what the keys keep apart, only in the answer; the tables stay as they are. With a second JOIN to readings you got the temperature of every room by name.

cards.question: What is a digital twin of a building?
answers: A copy of the building in data that follows what goes on in the real one
Something that sensors, a database and a picture together can make for a single room
A second, identical building built next to the first as a backup
The architect's 3D model, frozen at the day of the handover
cards.explanation: A twin follows the real building: sensors report, a database remembers, a picture shows it. A static 3D model does not follow anything.

cards.question: Which of these describe a data pipeline?
answers: A chain of steps that takes raw data to a stored, usable result
Something that runs the same way every time, for example on a new recording
A one-off manual copy and paste of numbers into a spreadsheet
The cable that connects a sensor to the internet
cards.explanation: A pipeline is a repeatable chain of steps. In session 5, run_twin did the whole chain for any door recording.

cards.question: ETL stands for extract, transform, load. Which steps belong where?
answers: Extract: reading the door CSV and asking Sensoto for the temperature
Transform: repairing miscounts and turning events into five-minute steps
Load: drawing the dashboard
Extract: writing the tables into the SQLite file
cards.explanation: Extract gets the raw data, transform cleans and reshapes it, load stores it (here in SQLite). Showing it comes after ETL.

cards.question: What does resampling do with door events?
answers: It turns events at irregular times into one value per regular step, such as five minutes
It needs a rule for each step, for example the last count in it
It removes the miscounts from the data
It fetches more events from the sensor
cards.explanation: resample("5min").last() took the count at the end of each five minutes. It changes the time steps, it does not repair anything.

cards.question: Which statements about a plausibility check are true?
answers: It looks for values that cannot be true, such as fewer than zero people in a room
A repaired value is possible, but not necessarily true
If it finds nothing, the data is guaranteed to be correct
It can tell exactly when a missed person walked in
cards.explanation: The check only sees impossible values. In the sample, two of three mistakes cancelled out, and the repair could not tell when the missed person had entered.
